1. Executive Summary & Project Objectives

In modern urban rail transit networks, unscheduled train withdrawals directly cause service disruptions, track congestion, passenger delays, and substantial operational maintenance penalties. The Air Production Unit (APU) compressor is a safety-critical subsystem that delivers compressed air to pneumatic braking assemblies, secondary suspension bellows, pantograph actuators, and automated passenger door mechanisms.

This academic research project establishes a reproducible, scientifically defensible predictive maintenance benchmark across real-world operational compressor telemetry from Metro do Porto, Portugal. Following a formal scientific audit, the project implements a Dual-Evaluation Framework that establishes empirical transparency between two fundamentally distinct operational tasks:

  • Task 1: Active Fault Detection & State Monitoring — Evaluates continuous state classification across both the 2-hour pre-failure lead window and the subsequent active failure outage duration.
  • Task 2: Anticipatory Pre-Failure Warning — Evaluates pure prognostic forecasting strictly during the documented 2-hour pre-failure window, with all observations during the active breakdown outage explicitly excluded from the positive test target.
Benchmark Scope: Compares three candidate deep learning architectures (LSTM, GRU, and TCN) across two full-resolution real-world APU compressor datasets (MetroPT-3 and MetroPT-2), evaluating a total of six independent experimental pipelines.

  • Dataset 2 (MetroPT-2): 7,116,940 raw records (711,694 timesteps at 10s intervals), 21 total columns (16 APU telemetry channels), 0 missing values.
  • Total Number of Images: 0 (The benchmark is purely multivariate continuous and discrete time-series sensor telemetry).
  • Class Target: Binary Classification (0 = Normal Operation, 1 = Failure Warning / Active State).

7. Proposed Methodology & Technical Details

The proposed methodology is structured into eight reproducible, mathematically rigorous engineering phases designed to guarantee absolute temporal isolation and prevent any data leakage:

Step-by-Step Methodology Details:

  1. Chunked Telemetry Ingestion & 10s Resampling: The raw datasets (10.77M and 7.12M rows logged at 1 Hz and sub-second intervals) exceed local memory capacity. We stream the CSV files in chunks of 500,000 rows and resample to regular 10-second intervals (0.1 Hz). Continuous thermodynamic signals (temperatures, pressures, flow rates) are aggregated via temporal mean; discrete binary control signals (COMP, DV_eletric, LPS) preserve their latest observed switch state. This reduces array size by 90% without compromising physical compressor pressure-flow dynamics.
  2. Defensible Failure Horizons & Target Construction: Based on official maintenance intervention records (Veloso et al., 2022; Jakobs et al., 2026), we establish a 2-hour pre-failure lead horizon:
    H_warn = [T_failure - 2 hours, T_failure]
    This provides maintenance dispatchers with an actionable warning window before safety shutdowns occur.
  3. Strict Chronological Splitting: To eliminate temporal and lookahead leakage, data is partitioned strictly chronologically:
    • MetroPT-3: Train (Jan 1 – Apr 17, 2022, 70%), Val (Apr 17 – May 8, 2022, 15%), Test (May 8 – Jun 2, 2022, 15%).
    • MetroPT-2: Train (Apr 28 – Jun 27, 2022, 65%), Val (Jun 27 – Jul 10, 2022, 15%), Test (Jul 10 – Jul 28, 2022, 20%).
  4. Leak-Free Normalization: Feature scaling parameters (mean and standard deviation) are fitted strictly on training data using StandardScaler and subsequently applied to validation and test splits:
    z = (x - mean_train) / std_train
  5. Memory-Efficient Sequence Windowing: Multivariate telemetry is windowed into sequences of length W = 60 timesteps (10 minutes of operational history) with a stride of S = 6 timesteps (1-minute step). A custom PyTorch SequenceWindowDataset indexes sequences on the fly, avoiding massive 3D tensor duplication in RAM.
  6. Balanced Training Sampling: Training sequences are balanced to 1:1 by exact random undersampling of healthy windows (N = 517 in MetroPT-3; N = 365 in MetroPT-2). Validation and test sets preserve their natural class distributions.
  7. Deep Learning Architectures: Three architectures were implemented in PyTorch:
    • LSTM: 2 stacked recurrent layers (hidden dimension 64, dropout 0.2) with a dense linear classification head.
    • GRU: 2 stacked gated recurrent layers (hidden dimension 64, dropout 0.2) with reset and update gates.
    • TCN (Temporal Convolutional Network): Dilated causal residual convolutions with dilation factors d in {1, 2, 4}, kernel size k = 3, channel progression [32, 64, 128], and global average pooling.
  8. Dual-Evaluation & Validation-Only Threshold Calibration: Models are evaluated separately on Task 1 (Active Fault State Monitoring) and Task 2 (Anticipatory Pre-Failure Warning). Decision thresholds are calibrated using unsupervised quantiles on healthy validation data (q90, q95, q98) to overcome the recall collapse of the default threshold boundary without test label leakage.

Confusion Matrix Diagnostic Takeaways:
  • MetroPT-2 In-Distribution Fault Tracking (Task 1): GRU and LSTM models achieve 100% recall (TP = 3,767, FN = 0, TN = 18,725, FP = 1,222) with 96.8% precision, while TCN detects 3,766 out of 3,767 positive windows (Recall = 99.97%). The active air-leak failure creates sustained pressure-cycle anomalies that all three temporal architectures identify reliably.
  • MetroPT-2 Anticipatory Early Warning (Task 2): When active outage windows are excluded, GRU and LSTM capture 100% of pre-failure lead windows (TP = 120, FN = 0) with false alarms restricted to 122 and 124 windows across 19,947 healthy observations (Test FPR ≈ 0.61%–0.62%). TCN detects 119 out of 120 windows (Recall = 99.17%, FP = 129, Test FPR ≈ 0.65%).
  • MetroPT-3 Out-of-Distribution Shift: When models trained on pneumatic air leaks encounter an unobserved lubrication failure (oil leak) in the test set, the default decision threshold (τ = 0.50) triggers zero true positives for LSTM (TP = 0, FP = 0) and GRU (TP = 0, FP = 29). TCN's dilated receptive fields capture 51 positive windows (TP = 51, FP = 72). Calibrating thresholds on validation quantiles restores operational sensitivity (Recall = 31.4%–35.0%) without test label leakage.

12. Physical & Algorithmic Findings & Limitations

1. Base-Rate Fallacy Explanation for Observed ~49.6% Precision

In MetroPT-2 Task 2, models achieved near-perfect sensitivity (GRU Recall = 100%, LSTM Recall = 100%, TCN Recall = 99.17%) while exhibiting precision of ~49.6%. This is a direct mathematical consequence of the base-rate effect under extreme class imbalance:

  • Pre-failure warning windows represent only 0.60% of the test population (N_pos = 120 vs. N_neg = 19,947, a 166:1 normal-to-fault ratio).
  • GRU generated only FP = 122 false alarms across 19,947 healthy windows, achieving an exceptionally low test False-Positive Rate of:
    FPR = FP / (TN + FP) = 122 / (19,825 + 122) = 122 / 19,947 ≈ 0.61%
  • Because healthy observations outnumber warning windows by 166 to 1, even a sub-1% false positive rate produces an absolute count of false alarms comparable to true events:
    Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 120 / (120 + 122) ≈ 49.59%

2. The Physical Barrier of Cross-Fault Generalization in MetroPT-3

In MetroPT-3, the training partition contained pneumatic Air Leak failures, while the held-out test partition contained an unobserved Oil Leak (lubrication breakdown):

  • Air leaks manifest through acute pressure drop cycles (TP2, TP3) and elevated duty cycles (COMP, Motor_current).
  • Oil leaks manifest through thermal degradation (Oil_temperature) and eventual float switch activation (Oil_level).
  • Models trained on pneumatic pressure drops exhibited severe generalization degradation when evaluated on lubrication failure. Under Task 2, pre-failure PR-AUC dropped to ~0.014–0.021. In Task 1, TCN achieved the highest PR-AUC (0.1939) and was the only model with positive recall at τ=0.50, demonstrating that dilated causal receptive fields may capture broader anomaly signals than recurrent baselines under distribution shift.

3. Validation Target FPR vs. Measured Test FPR (Seasonal Drift)

While validation quantiles targeted a 2.0% FPR at q98, measured test FPR increased to 7.3%–8.2%. This drift reflects seasonal transition into warmer weather in late May, which elevated ambient temperatures and normal compressor operating baselines relative to April. This finding emphasizes the operational necessity of continuous or adaptive threshold calibration over extended operating periods.

4. Methodological Limitations of Available Documented Events

The public benchmarks document a small number of physical failure incidents (N = 3 in MetroPT-3; N = 2 in MetroPT-2). In MetroPT-3, evaluating cross-fault generalization relies on a single test incident (N = 1 oil leak). Consequently, while the experimental design avoids temporal leakage, performance reflects the interaction between that specific physical incident and the training air leaks. Broad claims of generalizability across all arbitrary failure modes cannot be established without multi-year, multi-train fleet datasets.
